lesson.grammar_point: cleft sentences for emphasis (what ... is, it was ... that, all ... is)

listenings.text: Sure. What I run is a components plant outside Cleveland, about two hundred people, and I have had that job for six years. I am going to start there rather than at the beginning, and if you want the degree and the first two jobs I will come back to them. The year that matters is 2018, when the plant nearly closed. Nobody had a plan and nobody wanted to own it, so I stepped up before anybody offered me the job, and everything after that year has been a different role even though the title took two more years to catch up. If there is a through-line, it is that I have always been the person who fixes the thing nobody wants to own. That is true of the plant and it was true of the two jobs before it. That is probably two minutes. What would you like me to go deeper on?

Tell me about yourself is not a question. It is a test, and what it is testing is whether you can decide what matters. Nobody hands you a structure. It is an open space, and what you choose to put in it is the answer. Now, about the first ninety seconds. The room decides in the first ninety seconds how much of the rest of what you say it is going to believe, which is unfair and completely real. And most candidates spend those ninety seconds on the degree and the first job, which is the part nobody asked about and the part that is already on the form. One more thing, and I say this to every candidate who is interviewing in a second language. Do not apologize for your English. The apology costs you more than the mistake ever does. Nobody in that room expects perfect English. They expect a person who keeps going.

Researchers at a business school recorded around three hundred admissions interviews in which the candidate was speaking a second language, and then asked experienced interviewers to rate them without knowing what the study was about. The finding that surprised everybody is that grammatical mistakes had almost no measurable effect on the ratings at all. Two things did lower them. The first was apologizing for your own English, which happened in about a third of the recordings and which reliably pulled the score down. The second was rambling: answers that ran well past two minutes without arriving anywhere. And there is one more result worth reporting, because it goes against what most candidates believe. A pause before answering was read as thinking, not as difficulty. In several of the recordings it made the candidate sound more senior than the one who answered immediately.
